client: I've been really struggling lately with these final exams coming up, and I honestly don't know if talking about it is going to change anything. I got a low grade on my last psychology paper and it just kind of confirmed this feeling I have that no matter how hard I try, I'm going to fail. It's like this constant knot in my stomach that won't go away, even when I'm trying to sleep or just sit down and study.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling this way — carrying that knot of anxiety through your days and nights is genuinely exhausting, and I'm really glad you're here even if you're not sure it'll help. That thought, *"no matter how hard I try, I'm going to fail,"* is such a heavy one to carry, and I'd love to gently explore it with you, because one difficult grade on a paper is one data point — not a verdict on your future. What would you say to a close friend who told you that a single low grade meant they were destined to fail?

client: I mean, I'd probably tell a friend that one grade doesn't define them, that they should keep trying. But it feels different when it's me — like I know the "right" answer to give someone else, but I can't actually believe it for myself. It's like there's this wall between knowing something logically and actually feeling it in my gut.
therapist: What you're describing - that gap between knowing something and *feeling* it - is one of the most human experiences there is, and it doesn't mean you're broken or doing something wrong. That wall you're talking about is actually something we can work with together, because feelings often need more than logic — they need evidence gathered from your own lived experience over time. Can you think of a time in the past, maybe even outside of academics, where you kept trying at something difficult and it actually turned out better than you feared?

client: I mean... yeah, I guess there was this one time I had to give a presentation at work, and I was convinced I was going to completely fall apart in front of everyone. It actually went okay, better than I expected, but the thing is, when I think about that now, it still doesn't really connect to how I feel about school. Like my brain just says "that's different, that doesn't count," and I'm back to feeling like I'm going to fail no matter what I do.
therapist: Your brain dismissing that work presentation as "not counting" is actually a really important thing to notice — that's a classic move our anxious minds make to protect the story that failure is inevitable, because if evidence to the contrary "doesn't count," the belief never has to be challenged. What's fascinating is that you just caught your own mind doing it in real time, which takes real self-awareness. I'm curious — what do you think your brain is trying to protect you from by holding onto this belief that you'll fail no matter what?

client: I mean... I guess when you put it that way, it kind of makes sense, but it also feels a little too neat, you know? Like, maybe my brain isn't "protecting" anything — maybe I just actually do fail a lot, and the presentation went okay by luck. But if I'm being honest, I think there's something about... if I let myself believe I can succeed, and then I don't, that's so much worse than just expecting the worst from the start.
therapist: What you just said is incredibly insightful — that expecting the worst feels like a shield against the devastation of hoping and then being disappointed. That's not irrational at all; it's actually a very understandable way your mind has learned to protect you from pain, but the cost is that you're living under a storm cloud even on the days when the sun is out. I wonder, is the constant anxiety and dread you're feeling right now — that knot in your stomach — actually less painful than the risk of hoping, or is it possible the "protection" is costing you more than it's saving?

client: I mean... when you put it that way, I have to admit the knot in my stomach is pretty much constant, it's not like it ever really goes away. So maybe you're right that I'm not actually protecting myself from anything, I'm just... already in the pain I was trying to avoid. But it still feels terrifying to even consider hoping for things, because at least with the dread I know what I'm dealing with — hope feels like standing on the edge of something I could fall off of.
therapist: That image of standing on the edge is so vivid and real, and I want to honor how scary that feels — but I also want to gently point out that you've been describing someone who is *already* carrying enormous weight, already exhausted, already in pain, which means you've actually been surviving something really hard all along without giving yourself credit for it. Hope doesn't have to mean leaping off the edge all at once — it can start as something much smaller, like just allowing the *possibility* that this exam period might go differently than you fear. What might it look like to try just a tiny, low-stakes experiment with hope this week — something small enough that it doesn't feel like the edge of a cliff?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe it... but then this other part just immediately goes, "yeah, but what if this exam period is exactly as bad as I think it will be?" Like, what does a small experiment with hope even look like when every time I sit down to study I just freeze up and feel like I'm already failing? I guess I'm scared that if I let myself hope even a little and then it still goes wrong, that'll hurt more than just expecting the worst from the start.
therapist: You've actually just named something really important — that freezing when you sit down to study isn't laziness or proof you'll fail, it's anxiety doing what anxiety does, making the threat feel so overwhelming that your mind and body just lock up. A small experiment with hope doesn't have to mean believing you'll ace everything — it could be something as tiny as sitting down to study for just ten minutes with the intention of *noticing* what actually happens, rather than predicting it in advance. And if it does go wrong sometimes, we can look at that together — but I'm wondering, has every single study session ended in the worst possible outcome, or have there been moments, even small ones, where you got something done?

client: I mean... no, not every single session has been a complete disaster. There have been times where I actually got through a few pages or finished a problem set, but then I immediately think "well, that was a fluke" or "it wasn't good enough anyway." The ten-minute thing sounds simple, but I'm already imagining sitting down and just... spiraling into that same frozen panic, and I don't know if noticing it is going to make it feel any less awful.
therapist: You just did something really significant — you found real evidence that contradicts the story that every session fails, and then watched your mind immediately label it a "fluke," which is exactly the same move it made with your work presentation. That pattern of dismissing your own successes is worth holding onto, because it suggests the problem isn't your ability — it's a very persistent habit of discounting yourself. And you're right that noticing the spiral might not make it feel less awful at first, but I'm curious — what do you think it might be worth, even just a little, to start building a small collection of moments your brain *can't* so easily dismiss?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it — like, intellectually I can see the pattern you're describing. But honestly, my first reaction is that building some kind of "collection" sounds a little forced, like I'd just be manufacturing evidence to trick myself into feeling better. And I'm not sure I trust that, because my brain would probably just find a way to dismiss the whole collection too.
therapist: Your skepticism here is actually really healthy — you're not looking for a quick trick or a way to paper over something real, and that tells me you want something that actually works, not just something that feels good for a moment. What I'd gently push back on is the idea that noticing your own successes is "manufacturing" evidence — it's actually just *balancing* the ledger, because right now your brain is very efficiently collecting all the failures and losses while automatically shredding the wins. What do you think it would mean about you if some of those dismissed moments — the finished problem sets, the okay presentation — were actually real and not flukes?

client: I mean... if those things were real and not flukes, I guess it would mean I'm not as incompetent as I feel most of the time. But that's actually kind of a scary thought, because if I'm not incompetent, then I don't have an excuse anymore for why things are still so hard. Like, it's almost easier to believe I'm just bad at this stuff than to accept that I'm capable and still struggling.
therapist: What you just said is one of the most honest and courageous things you could have shared — that believing in your own incompetence has actually been functioning as a kind of explanation, even a comfort, because "I'm just bad at this" is a simpler story than "I'm capable and still finding this genuinely hard." But being capable and struggling aren't opposites — in fact, struggle is often what capability actually looks like from the inside, especially under real pressure like finals. I'm wondering, what might it feel like to hold both of those things at once — that you have real ability *and* that this is legitimately difficult — without one canceling the other out?

client: Honestly, when you put it that way, something kind of shifted for me just now, like a small crack in something I've been holding really tightly. But I also don't fully trust that feeling, because I've told myself I'm capable before and then failed anyway, and that just made things worse. I guess I'm scared that if I let myself believe I'm capable and I still mess up these finals, I won't have any explanation left, and that feels even more terrifying than just accepting I'm not good enough.
therapist: That small crack you're feeling is real and worth honoring, even if it feels fragile right now — and I want to gently offer that failing at something while being capable isn't the same as having no explanation, because "this was hard, I was anxious, and I'm still learning" is actually a more truthful and compassionate explanation than "I'm just not good enough." The terror you're describing makes complete sense, but I notice you've been carrying the "I'm not good enough" story for a while now, and it hasn't actually protected you from pain or made the knot in your stomach go away. I'm curious — if messing up these finals didn't have to mean anything final or definitive about who you are, what do you think you might be able to let yourself try?
